predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2, in-text citation and reference list
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text cites 'Beck et al., 2025' but the reference list shows 'Beck et al., 2024' (the actual NeurIPS 2024 paper). The year is inconsistent; the correct citation year should be 2024.

The footnote states 'This Gaussian kernel smoothing not only converges to the true conditional expectation E(V|K) when n → ∞ and β = √n [Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1964]'. The Nadaraya–Watson estimator's consistency is established under general bandwidth conditions, not for the specific formula β = √n without regard to the dimension of the key space. Citing these works for that exact parameterisation is a misattribution.

The footnote claims 'A two-layer feed-forward network and a key-value associative memory are interchangeable as shown in Sukhbaatar et al. [2019]'. That paper introduces persistent memory vectors concatenated to the key-value set, not a dense network; the claimed interchangeability is not supported by the cited work, which constitutes an overstatement.

The text states: 'transformers completely fail to improve and show severe performance collapse as more demonstrations are provided (red curves).' However, Figure 3 (Banking77 semantic labels) shows the transformer accuracy rising from ~0.58 to ~0.70, a clear improvement. The blanket claim of 'completely fail to improve' is contradicted by the figure.

The abstract claims 'universal superiority in zero-shot and few-shot scenarios'. The paper only evaluates few-shot in-context learning; no zero-shot classification experiments are reported. 'Universal superiority' is an unsupported overstatement.

The section states 'our results definitively prove that data scaling alone cannot close the gap, as the fundamental architectural limitations of transformers make them inherently inferior for these tasks regardless of training data quantity.' The experiments only test up to 8× more training tokens (8T) and employ a confounded setup (different attention type and training context length). The conclusion is not 'definitively' proven and extends beyond the evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 6.1, comparison of 8T transformer with Memory Mosaics v2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The 8T transformer ('transformer large*') uses grouped-query attention and was trained with an 8k context length, whereas the 1T transformer uses multi-head attention and 4k context. The comparison to Memory Mosaics v2 is therefore confounded: the improved performance of the 8T model cannot be attributed solely to data scaling, undermining the analysis of 'data scaling alone'.

The claim that Gaussian kernel regression converges when β = √n ignores the dimension d of the key vectors. The Nadaraya–Watson estimator requires a bandwidth schedule that depends on dimension (e.g., h ∼ n^{-1/(d+4)}), which would correspond to β ∼ n^{2/(d+4)}. Stating β = √n as a universal sufficient condition is mathematically inaccurate without further assumptions.

The abstract asserts that Memory Mosaics v2 'completely eliminat[es] the need for additional training data that transformers require'. This absolute statement is not supported by the results, which only compare a few training budgets; it ignores scenarios where more training data could improve transformers beyond the tested range.
